# The Four Minutes

The clock at the end of Mercy Street was four minutes slow. Everyone knew it, including the man who came twice a year to wind it, though he was under the impression that only he knew.

The clock had once belonged to a department store. When the store shut, the building became a pharmacy on the ground floor and six apartments above. The clock stayed where it was, bolted to the brick over the old entrance, which was now a wall. People still said, “Meet me under the clock,” and stood in front of the wall feeling a little foolish.

On the first Tuesday in November, a woman called Ruth arrived with a ladder and a municipal work order. The order said REMOVE REDUNDANT TIMEPIECE. In the space marked REASON, someone had typed INACCURATE.

She was extending the ladder when a man carrying two cups of coffee stopped beside her.

“How inaccurate?” he asked.

“Four minutes.”

“Is it getting worse?”

“Apparently not.”

He considered this. “That’s quite good, then.”

Ruth had worked for the city for nineteen years. She knew the difference between a man who wanted an answer and a man who had brought a second coffee in the hope of having a conversation. She took the coffee.

His name was Daniel. He used to meet his wife under the clock on Tuesdays, he said. She finished work at five and took the bus into town. He walked from the print shop. They had dinner at the place that was now a shop selling expensive soap.

“And now?” Ruth asked.

“Now I buy a coffee for myself and, as you can see, make poor decisions about the second.”

He said it lightly. Ruth looked down at the lid. Someone had drawn a small S on it in blue marker.

“Sugar,” Daniel said.

“I didn’t ask.”

“You looked like you might.”

She drank it. There was too much sugar.

From the top of the ladder she could see into the first-floor apartment. A child in a school uniform was trying to feed a piece of toast to a sleeping dog. The child looked up, startled, and Ruth raised her work order in explanation. The child raised the toast.

The clock’s casing was held shut by two screws, one of which had been painted over so many times it looked like a lump of chewing gum. Ruth scraped the paint away. Inside, someone had tucked a folded receipt between the casing and the mechanism. It was from the department store, dated thirty-one years earlier, for two pillowcases and a lamp. On the back, in pencil, was written: *If you alter the hands, do not alter the pendulum.*

She called her supervisor.

“Can I correct it instead?”

“Is that cheaper?”

“Almost certainly.”

“Then why did we send a van?”

“You always send a van.”

There was a silence during which Ruth could hear him eating something crisp. “Use your judgment,” he said at last, in the tone of a man who expected not to hear about it again.

At noon, Ruth moved the minute hand forward. The mechanism accepted the change without complaint. She put the receipt back where she had found it and climbed down.

Daniel was still there, sitting on the low wall outside the pharmacy.

“You’ve fixed it,” he said.

“Yes.”

He checked his watch. The clock and the watch agreed. He put his hands in his coat pockets.

“My wife used to set her watch by that clock,” he said. “She knew it was slow. She’d do it while I was standing there telling her it was slow.”

“Why?”

“I thought she was doing it to annoy me.” He smiled. “That was a perfectly good reason, as far as she was concerned.”

Ruth folded the ladder. Across the street, a delivery driver was arguing with a parking meter. A pharmacist came outside to eat an apple. Overhead, the child had opened the window, and the dog, now awake, put its nose out into the cold.

“Her bus was always late,” Daniel said. “No more than a few minutes, usually. She hated making anybody wait. One day I told her I went by the clock, so as far as I was concerned she was early.”

“Did you?”

“No. I went by my watch. I liked having a few minutes to stand here and look for her.”

He sounded surprised to have said it. Ruth busied herself with a strap that had twisted around the ladder.

At twelve fifteen, Daniel said goodbye. He thanked her for drinking the coffee. She thanked him for buying it. He went away in the direction of the expensive soap, walking a little sideways at first as he tucked one glove into the other.

Ruth put the ladder in the van. She completed the work order, crossing out REMOVE and writing ADJUSTED. She was about to start the engine when she noticed something in the side mirror.

A woman had stopped under the clock. She was looking up at it, then at her phone. She looked up again. The expression on her face was not annoyance but calculation. A moment later she put her phone away and ran toward the bus stop.

Ruth watched her catch the bus.

The following Tuesday, Ruth was back on Mercy Street to replace a bent street sign. It was nearly five when she finished. As she came around the corner, she saw Daniel by the wall with a coffee in each hand. He held one out to her.

“No sugar this time,” he said. “I had to guess about the milk.”

There was a little too much milk, but she didn’t tell him that. She had parked on a yellow line and meant to explain that she could only stay a minute. Instead she asked him what his wife’s name was.

“Susan,” he said. Then he took a sip of coffee and added, “She couldn’t stand that restaurant, by the way. We went every week for eleven years before she told me.”

Ruth laughed. Across the street a bus pulled in, and Daniel turned, without quite meaning to, to see who got off. Ruth stayed until the next bus came.
